open-question.question: The goal excludes directories "listed in ## Milestone History", but that section's headings carry only the integer number and a title (### Milestone N — Title), never the directory name, while the ## Completed Milestones table pairs the number with the backticked directory path. Which structure, and which field of it, does the skill match a milestone_<NN>_<slug> directory against to decide it is done: the number in the History headings, the path in the Completed Milestones table, or both?

The lowest-numbered pick needs a rule for reading the number out of milestone_<NN>_<slug>, and the only such rule in the skill today (strip leading zeros, compare as integers) lives inside the multiple-candidate branch that is being removed. Does the integer rule survive as a standalone sentence of the candidate step, and does a directory whose prefix does not parse as an integer get skipped or stop the run?
open-question.alternative: Keep the zero-stripped integer rule as a standalone sentence of the candidate step, and define candidates as directories matching `milestone_<digits>_<slug>` only. A directory whose prefix is not all digits never matches the pattern, so it is quietly left out of the candidate set. It is the smallest edit that still orders correctly past milestone 99. It moves the existing sentence out of the branch being removed, matches the parse rule `/define-milestone-goal` already uses for max-plus-one, and adds no new stop to a skill whose goal allows exactly two. A misnamed directory (for example `milestone_3a_fix` or one created by hand) is ignored with no signal. The user may then wonder why a milestone they defined is never activated, and the skill leaves no trace explaining it.

Keep the integer rule as a standalone sentence, and make any `milestone_*` directory whose number does not parse as an integer stop the run with a message naming the directory, before anything is written. A malformed directory is never silently passed over or mis-ordered. The user hears about it right away, and an unattended `claude -p` chain fails loudly instead of activating some other milestone. It adds a third stop condition when the goal says the skill stops in only two cases, so the goal text or a recorded decision would need to widen that. It also halts every activation over a stray directory that `/define-milestone-goal`'s naming rule should never have produced.

Keep the integer rule as a standalone sentence, leave directories whose prefix does not parse out of the candidate set, and have the run print one advisory line naming each skipped directory next to the terse `Milestone activated.` line. The run still finishes under the goal's two stop cases, and the user still learns that a directory was ignored. This fits the terse-reporting rule's allowance for decision-critical advisories that git does not record. It adds a second line to the success-path output and a new reporting branch to the skill, all for a case the project's own naming makes nearly impossible. It also stretches the "one fixed identifier-free status line" rule toward per-item output.

Drop the explicit number rule and pick the candidate whose directory name sorts first. This relies on `/define-milestone-goal` always zero-padding the number to two digits. The candidate step needs no parse sentence and no handling for unparseable prefixes, so it is the shortest possible text. Ordering breaks at milestone 100: `milestone_100_…` sorts before `milestone_99_…` because define pads to two digits, not three. The order would also differ silently from the integer rule `/define-milestone-goal` uses, and a misnamed directory would land at an arbitrary place in the order.

open-question.question: Once the skill only proceeds when the pointer reads none and always overwrites it with a path, the commit procedure's dirty-own-path guard can no longer fire, so the "No change — the pointer already named that milestone" line in the confirm step becomes unreachable. Does that branch stay as a defensive fallback or is it removed along with the prompts?
open-question.alternative: Leave step 5's no-change branch as it is, with its current example line `No change — the pointer already named that milestone; nothing committed.`, and remove only the confirmation and choice prompts from step 2. This is the smallest edit. The skill keeps the same reporting shape as every other committing skill (define-milestone-goal, modify-milestone-goal, specify-milestone-starting-state, init-milestone-base-workflow, and review-milestone-requirements all carry a distinct no-change line for when the dirty-own-path guard fires). It also still covers a case the premise overlooks. Say the committed README already points at milestone X and someone resets it to none by hand without committing. The skill then writes X back, the file matches HEAD again, `git status --porcelain` shows it clean, and the guard fires. So the branch is rare but can still be reached. The reason in the example line no longer fits how the guard can actually fire. Step 1 has just confirmed the pointer read none, so "the pointer already named that milestone" contradicts what the skill saw. A reader could also take the branch as a sign that re-activating the current milestone is still a supported path, when the non-interactive design rules that out.

Keep the no-change branch in step 5 but rewrite its example reason to the one case that can still reach it. The pointer the skill wrote matches the last commit because an uncommitted edit had reset it to none. The skill still prints no terse line and commits nothing. The skill still says exactly what happens when the guard fires, so it never prints `Milestone activated.` for a run that recorded nothing. The message also tells the truth about the one real cause, and the reporting shape stays consistent with the other committing skills. It adds prose about a hand-edit case that almost never happens, to a skill whose milestone goal is simplification. It also puts a claim about how the workflow is misused into runtime prose, and that claim has to be kept accurate if the pointer or commit mechanics change later.

Delete step 5's no-change paragraph along with the prompts. The skill then prints only `Milestone activated.`, and the rare case where nothing gets committed is left to the commit procedure's own instruction to report the no-op and return cleanly. The skill gets shorter and matches the new design, where every run that passes step 1 writes a new path and commits it. That removes the misleading reason and the idea that re-activation is still possible. The uncommitted-reset case can still reach the guard, and step 5 would then no longer say what to print. The runner could print `Milestone activated.` for a run that committed nothing, or produce a free-form message. That breaks the rule that no-op passes print one distinct line. It is also the only committing skill that would lack a no-change branch.

open-question.question: With the choice removed, a defined milestone that the user no longer wants but never finished is picked on every run and blocks every higher-numbered one, since the skill stops only on a non-none pointer or on no candidate. Is that accepted as-is, with deleting the directory as the way out, or does the skill or its documentation need to state how to skip such a milestone?

The README template in init-milestone-base-workflow says the ## Completed Milestones table is written by /goto-next-milestone, but the finish skill writes it and goto-next-milestone only reads it at most. Is correcting that note in scope for this milestone, given it sits outside the files the goal lists?

The goal names docs/skill-reference.md, docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, and the host trees as the documents to update, while CLAUDE.md's pipeline listing describes the skill and its invariants section records every retired interactive behaviour elsewhere as a must-not-restore rule, and docs/workflow.md says the skill advances the pointer. Do CLAUDE.md (pipeline line and a new invariant on the lowest-numbered pick and the retired prompts) and docs/workflow.md get updated in this milestone too?
